## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The X-25 is not a research aircraft in the sense the rest of this series uses.** It is a civil production
design, sold as plans to amateur builders, ordered in modified form and given a designation. Little was
developed for the two aircraft that flew, and the one new element the record names, the automatically
deploying rotor of the unpowered gyro-chute, is not known to have flown with a pilot, in [Jenkins, Landis and
Miller][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. No aerodynamic result is recorded. Treating it through a keystone derivation implies a design
process that did not take place, and this article's derivations describe **the concept** rather than an
engineering effort that anyone performed on this airframe.

**The keystone was never in doubt.** Autorotation was understood in the 1920s, and Cierva's C.4 made the
first documented autogyro flight in January 1923, in the [autogyro][ref_autogyro] entry. The X-25 did not test whether
a rotor autorotates, and an article that dimensions the rotor as though it were being designed misrepresents
what the money bought.

**The designation is the anomaly, not the aircraft.** The X-series designations went to aircraft meant to
explore new flight regimes or untried technologies, in [Jenkins, Landis and
Miller][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. The X-25s that flew were modified catalogue items with serial
numbers applied to them. This is a genuine finding about how the designation system drifted, and it sits with the
other evidence the closing article of this series will assemble.

**Finally, the comparison at the centre of this article may be unfair in one direction.** A parachute is compared
against a rotor at equal weight, but the parachute is also the reserve. If the rotor follows the parachute
in the sequence and does not replace it, the crewman carries both and the mass comparison should
arguably be against the marginal mass of the rotor rather than against the canopy that is carried
regardless. **On that accounting the rotor is worse than this article makes it look**, not better.

## The Source Base

**The record for the aircraft itself is the thinnest in the series so far, and the record for the physics around it is not.**
That asymmetry shapes the whole article and is worth stating plainly, so that a reader does not have to
infer it from the reference list.

**The vehicle itself has essentially no technical literature.** One research record cited in this article carries Bensen in its title, which is the chapter on Igor Bensen and the gyrocopter in a history of the type, [Chapter 11 IGOR BENSEN 2003][research_chapter_11_2003], and none carries the X-25 or the Discretionary Descent Vehicle. **Three** concern a flying rotor seat, which are [Barzda 1970][research_barzda_1970] and [Hollrock and Barzda 1972][research_hollrock_barzda_1972] on the SAVER and [Gross and Mawhinney 1970][research_gross_mawhinney_1970] on the AERCAB flying ejection seat, rather than the X-25. There is no flight test
report, no aerodynamic data report and no programme summary in the open literature reached here.
**The specifications in this article come from museum fact sheets and reference compilations, not from primary documents**,
and where those disagree the article says so rather than choosing.

**The supporting physics is abundant and that asymmetry is the point.** Autorotation, the autogiro, momentum
theory, blade element theory, parachutes and escape systems are all well documented from the 1920s onward.
**The article can derive everything about the concept and can verify almost nothing about the aircraft.**

**The research records are listed cluster by cluster under The Contemporary Literature**, including the period reports, the work of the intervening decades and the standard atmosphere on which every number in this article rests.

**The research survey holds 2,707 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 828 are report primaries, being 30.6 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2005.** Of the 2,679 dated records, 430 were published in 1968 or earlier, the year the X-25 first flew, being 16.1 percent, and 1,152 were published in 2015 or later, being 43.0 percent.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The NACA autogiro and autorotation reports that carry this article's keystone are report primaries under that rule. The rule does not reach the period journal papers**, such as [Glauert 1927][research_glauert_1927] and [de la Cierva 1930][research_de_la_cierva_1930] on the theory of the autogiro, so 30.6 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

**The keystone is thin on primary sources.** Autorotation carries 166 research records and 27 of them are report primaries, which is 16.3 percent against 30.6 percent for the survey as a whole. A record is an autorotation record when its title contains a word beginning autorotat, the word auto-rotative, a windmill or windmilling brake or rotor, or a power-off descent or rotor.

**The likely reason is a vocabulary that spans both eras.** Autorotation is a word the 1930s used and the
2020s still use, and on that shared word **the larger and better-indexed modern computational literature
simply outnumbers the period work**. That is an inference about the literature and not a measurement of it.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group, and where a row adds terms after the words or else, a title carrying one of those terms is counted as well.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| rotor spin-up and prerotation | prerotation, pre-rotation, prerotator, spin-up, rotor starting, starting torque, rotor run-up | 2 |
| stored rotor energy | rotor, blade together with inertia, kinetic energy, stored energy, or else autorotative index, flywheel | 4 |
| the flying rotor seat | SAVER, flying ejection seat, rescue autogyro, rotor seat | 3 |
| gyroplane safety and accidents | gyroplane, autogyro, autogiro, gyrocopter together with safety, accident, crash, airworthiness | 3 |
| the glide of an autorotating rotor | autorotating, autorotation, autorotative, gyroplane, autogyro, autogiro together with glide, gliding | 2 |
| cutting away a parachute | parachute, canopy together with cutaway, cut away, jettison, disconnect | 0 |
| gyroplane and autorotation training | gyroplane, autogyro, autogiro, autorotation together with training, trainer, instructor, test standards | 7 |

**Rotor spin-up and prerotation stands at two records, and neither is the case this article needs.** One concerns the engine loads of prerotating an autogyro rotor, [Czyż et al. 2016][research_czyz_usiak_2016], and one the control of the blades while a helicopter rotor is spun up in wind, [Kargaev et al. 2025][research_kargaev_korsun_2025]. No title in the survey names the spin-up of a rotor deployed in descent, although the deployable rotors of the SAVER and of the rotary decelerators under The Contemporary Literature must perform one. The word prerotation also names the prerotation of landing gear wheels and of the human trunk. That gap is the reason the spin-up section of this article reasons from energy rather than from measurement.

**Stored rotor energy appears to stand at four records and does not really.** The relevant work exists and is cited, but it sits inside the autorotation and blade-motion literature rather than beside it, because a paper on autorotative landing is a paper about spending exactly that energy. A dedicated heading for it is nearly empty while the subject is well covered. **A thin heading is not the same thing as a thin subject**, and the distinction is easy to get wrong in the direction of claiming a gap that is not there.

One further caution belongs here. The word flywheel also names
**flywheel energy storage for spacecraft and power grids**, meaning containment rings and composite burst
testing, which is a different discipline that happens to store energy in something that spins.
**That literature is a homonym of this subject rather than a part of it**, and no record of it is counted
here.

**The flying rotor seat, the class to which the SAVER belongs, stands at three records**, given above, and **cutting away a parachute stands at no record**, although it would be the irreversible step in any deployment sequence that included it.

**Gyroplane safety stands at three records.** They are [Doberentz et al. 2020][research_doberentz_geile_2020], [Houston et al. 1998][research_houston_spathopoulos_1998] and [Practice for Continued Airworthiness][research_practice_for], and no title among them compares trained with untrained pilots, which is why the training inference under Epistemic State is labelled as an inference.

**The glide of an autorotating rotor stands at two records**, the flight measurement of an autogiro's gliding performance in [Wheatley 1933][research_wheatley_1933] and a controller for steep glide slopes of an unmanned gyroplane in [Wu 2015][research_wu_2015], so the lift-to-drag ratio of 4 on which the range figures rest is assumed rather than taken from a measured X-25 polar.

**Gyroplane and autorotation training stands at seven records**, three of them the practical test standards for rotorcraft pilots and instructors and the rest on autorotation training in helicopters, so the subject the programme's testing addressed is among the thinnest here.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Its 2,707 records come from NASA's Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center and the journal literature registered with Crossref. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Occupant, crash and vehicle also name road traffic safety, landing also names knee and ankle loading in sport, and Parachute is also the name of a cardiac device, a heart valve, a band and a form of executive compensation. Vortex ring also names the quantised vortex rings of superfluid helium, samara also names the Samara Region, and canopy also names the crown of a tree. Autorotation also names the rotation of a telephone screen and of the jaw in surgery, height velocity also names the growth rate of children, and descent also names human gait. Prerotation also names the prerotation of landing gear wheels and tyres, of the human trunk, of pump impellers and of signal constellations in wireless networks, and rotor also names the rotors of electric machines, wave energy turbines, gyroscopes and industrial machinery. Drag coefficient also names the drag of sediment and process particles, of the sea surface in meteorology and of the ether in relativity. Electrical power systems, spaceflight outside the atmosphere, the testing and design of ordnance and the engineering of airfield landing mats are excluded as well. Correction, erratum, clarification, retraction and withdrawal notices, figure, table and supplementary-material records, peer-review reports and journal front matter are excluded too, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of it and its author's closure or reply are research works, since each argues about a result, and they are admitted when their subject is, while an unsigned discussion and a referee's report on a manuscript are not. Dictionary entries, advertisements and fiction are excluded for the same reason. The residual cluster admits only flight measurement and performance method, the descent, spinning and recovery of aircraft and other bodies, high-altitude aerodynamics and general aerodynamic texts, and fixed-wing work on supersonic and hypersonic flight, missiles and stores, engines, avionics, structures or operations, with no tie to a rotor, a descent or an escape, is not admitted to it or to any other cluster. The same rule excludes, from every cluster, fixed-wing electric and hybrid-electric aircraft, electric machines, the avionics and the operations and markets of unmanned aircraft and air mobility, and the supersonic drag of bodies and projectiles. It also excludes the landing autonomy, guidance, sensing and path planning of unmanned aircraft even when the vehicle is a rotorcraft, the structures, loads, controls, generators and floating platforms of wind turbines and every vertical-axis turbine, the drive trains, gears, lubrication, engines, ice protection, landing gear and cargo equipment of rotorcraft, the stresses and construction of propeller blades, open rotors and propfans, fixed-wing high lift, landing gear, arresting gear and runway operations, the noise of fixed-wing aircraft and engines and occupational noise exposure, simulator engineering and the administration of training, powered rocket landing, glide weapons, the imaging payloads of parafoils, the network coverage of landing sites, hearing protection and speech reception in aircraft, the quality assurance of manufacture, and airships and balloons. Conference proceedings, symposium volumes, appendices, patent notices and book reviews are excluded as parts of works or notices rather than works. Reference and definition entries such as glossaries, news items and announcements, and a second deposit of a document already counted are not admitted either, because none of them is a separate research work.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Injury biomechanics under blunt impact, parachute physiology and equipment, helmet-mounted display optics, bird and insect flight aerodynamics, classical vortex rings in fluid mechanics and combustion, kites and tethered autogyros for airborne wind energy, autorotation used to harvest energy and the drag of projectiles at low speed each share either the physics of a rotor, a descent or a body in flight, or the human side of an escape, with this subject, so each is kept and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, from the public record.** Three X-25 type aircraft were ordered in early 1968 under the
Discretionary Descent Vehicle programme, in the [X-25A][ref_nmusaf_x25a] fact sheet, and they were the basic
X-25 gyro-chute, the X-25A and the X-25B. The X-25A, serial 68-10770, first flew on 5 June 1968. The X-25B,
serial 68-10771, first flew on 5 June 1968 by [Guinness World Records][ref_guinness_x25b], the date the
inventory gives for the type, and on 23 January 1968 in the [Bensen B-8][ref_bensen_b8] entry, which cites
no source for it. The Guinness maximum takeoff weight of 547 pounds is the X-25A figure in the fact sheet, so
Guinness may not be independent of the inventory, and the adopted date rests in the end on that one
monograph. Both aircraft derive from Bensen B-8 family designs. Testing addressed piloting technique and
training requirements, and the fact sheet reports that pilots could be trained quickly and easily. No
full-scale operational test was performed. Funding ended with the American withdrawal from Vietnam, and the
fact sheet adds doubts about operational feasibility.
The X-25A is held by the National Museum of the United States Air Force and the X-25B by the Air Force Flight
Test Museum at Edwards, in [Jenkins, Landis and Miller][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. The Kaman SAVER
flew towed on 28 December 1971 and with a telescoping rotor on 10 January 1972, and was cancelled, in the
[Kaman KSA-100 SAVER][ref_kaman_saver] entry.

**Engineering analysis, derived here and checkable.** The equivalence between the autorotation ratio of 1.8
and a disc-referred drag coefficient of 1.23 is algebra containing no fitted quantity. The finding that an
autorotating rotor descends faster than a personnel canopy at equal weight follows from disc loading alone.
The glide range figures follow from an assumed lift-to-drag ratio of 4. The spin-up energy of about 57 feet
of ideal height loss follows from an assumed blade mass and tip speed. The SAVER descent rate of 56 feet per
second follows from documented weight and rotor diameter and is the least assumption-dependent number in the
article. The statement that a rotor at Martian density descends about ten times faster is the same
square-root relation evaluated at one percent of sea-level density and assumes nothing else,
**though it is an illustration of the relation and not a claim about any particular Mars vehicle**, which
would fly a rotor sized for that atmosphere.

**Assumed, and marked as such throughout.** The escape-configuration gross weight of 350 pounds. The
lift-to-drag ratio of 4. The best-glide speed of 45 miles per hour. The blade mass of 12 pounds each and tip
speed of 400 feet per second. The canopy comparison figures of 28 foot nominal diameter, 250 pound suspended
weight and a drag coefficient of 0.75. The blade chord of 7 inches. The rotor and parachute assembly masses
of 38 and 28 pounds. **None of these is a measurement of an X-25.**

**Inference, and labelled as inference.** That the programme's testing concerned training rather than
aerodynamics is an inference from the record's statement that the aircraft were used to evaluate piloting
technique and training requirements, combined with the absence of any aerodynamic finding, and the one
training result the record reports is favourable. That the doubts about operational feasibility concerned
the deployment sequence, the rotor's mass alongside a parachute or the stowage geometry is an inference from
this article's analysis, since the fact sheet names the doubts without describing them. That the ram-air
parachute is the historical answer to the Discretionary Descent Vehicle question is an inference from
capability comparison, not from any documented decision connecting the two.

**Two further inferences come from the contemporary survey and are labelled here because they are the article's strongest claims and its least documented.**
That a multirotor cannot autorotate follows from the stored-energy and disc-loading relations this article
derives, applied to a configuration those relations describe accurately, but
**no source consulted here states it as a finding and the airworthiness literature treats redundancy as a design choice rather than as a concession**.
And that the gyroplane's safety reputation bears on a crewman with no rotorcraft training is an
inference from the type's general reputation and from the contemporary safety literature,
**not from any study that compares trained and untrained gyroplane pilots**, which would be the evidence the
claim needs.

The vehicle-by-vehicle programme record for the X-series generally is [Jenkins, Landis and Miller on the
American X-vehicles][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003].

**What the record does not settle.** Whether the X-25 rotors were the 20 foot rotor of the standard B-8M.
Whether the engine was 72 or 90 horsepower. Which of the X-25A and X-25B flew first. What became of the third
aircraft, the gyro-chute. What the doubts about operational feasibility were. Whether the escape sequence included a parachute cutaway at all, and whether any
part of it was demonstrated below full scale.
Whether any quantitative descent or glide measurement was taken and survives in a closed report.

**Written from current knowledge.** The contemporary survey postdates the editorial date of this article.

## Out of Scope

The detailed aeroelastic behaviour of wooden rotor blades. Ejection seat dynamics and the injury mechanisms
of the ejection itself. The combat search and rescue apparatus the programme was meant to supplement. The
amateur-built rotorcraft accident record, which is substantial and is a different subject. The full history
of the Cierva autogiro. Powered-lift and compound rotorcraft. The detailed design of ram-air canopies. Wind
turbine engineering beyond the identity of the flow state.

## Conclusion

**The Bensen X-25 showed that pilots could learn the machine, and it never reached the escape it was for.**

The programme was framed as giving a descending crewman a choice, in [Jenkins, Landis and
Miller][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. The arithmetic shows that an autorotating
rotor is a worse decelerator than the parachute it was to replace, by nine percent at equal weight and
twenty-nine percent as flown, and that everything it offers comes from the fact that it is a wing rather
than a brake. **Seven and a half miles from ten thousand feet is the whole product.**

The obvious objection, that a rotor must be spun up while a canopy merely inflates,
**does not survive being written down**. Fifty-seven feet of ideal height loss is cheap. The difficulty was
never energetic, and on the record it was not training either, since the one test result reported is that
pilots learned the X-25 with ease. The programme ended because the air war that motivated it was
winding down and because of doubts about its operational feasibility, and the gyro-chute that embodied the
escape has no recorded piloted flight. By this article's inference the doubts had ground. The rotor buys
range and not a softer landing, weighs about as much as the parachute it accompanies, would need much heavier
blades or an engine to fold into a seat, and in any sequence through an open canopy would require cutting a
working parachute away.

**The question was good and it was eventually answered by fabric.** A ram-air canopy reaches nearly the same
glide ratio with no rigid structure, no spin-up and, by inference, less training, and guided airdrop has since removed the
pilot from the loop as well.
**The rotor's physics did not die. It went into wind energy, where the windmill brake state is the design condition rather than an emergency.**

The next article in this series takes up the Schweizer X-26 Frigate.

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 44 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 44, 23 are established and 21 are bespoke.
Quantities are in United States customary units, with weight in pounds, length in feet, speed in feet per second and density in slugs per cubic foot, and the escape weight of 350 pounds, the rotor diameter of 20 feet, the blade mass of 12 pounds, the tip speed of 400 feet per second, the blade chord of 7 inches and the lift-to-drag ratio of 4 are values the article assumes, while $\gamma$ is the glide angle and $\gamma_L$ the Lock number.

**Equation 1, In-Plane Force on a Blade Element.**
The net force in the plane of rotation on a blade element is the in-plane component of its lift less that of its drag at the inflow angle.

$$
dF_{x} = dL \sin\phi - dD \cos\phi
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Equilibrium Inflow Angle of an Autorotating Element.**
An element neither drives nor retards the rotor when the tangent of its inflow angle equals its section drag-to-lift ratio.

$$
\tan\phi = \frac{dD}{dL} = \frac{C_d}{C_l}
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Torque Balance of an Autorotating Rotor.**
A rotor in steady autorotation turns at the speed at which the moments of the in-plane forces of its driving and driven regions cancel over the disc.

$$
\int_{0}^{R} r \, dF_{x} = 0
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Disc Area and Hover Induced Velocity.**
The actuator-disc result gives the induced velocity a rotor needs in hover from its weight, the air density and its disc area.
[Leishman's helicopter aerodynamics][book_leishman_2006]
[Johnson's helicopter theory][book_johnson_1980]
[Castles and De Leeuw 1953][research_castles_de_leeuw_1953]

$$
A = \pi R^2, \qquad v_h = \sqrt{\frac{W}{2 \rho A}}
\tag{4}
$$

*Equation 5, Bespoke Disc Area of the X-25B Rotor.*
The disc area follows from a rotor diameter the article takes as 20 feet, since the record does not settle whether the X-25 used the standard B-8M rotor.

$$
A = \pi (10 \, \text{ft})^2 = 314.2 \, \text{ft}^2
\tag{5}
$$

*Equation 6, Bespoke Hover Induced Velocity of the X-25B.*
The actuator-disc induced velocity at an escape weight the article assumes as 350 pounds on the taken disc at sea-level density is about 15 feet per second.

$$
v_h = \sqrt{\frac{350}{2 (0.002377)(314.2)}} = 15.3 \, \text{ft/s}
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Momentum Theory Thrust in the Windmill Brake State.**
In the windmill brake state momentum theory gives the thrust in terms of the descent speed and the induction factor $a$.

$$
T = 2 \rho A V_d^2 \, a (1 - a)
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Descent Ratio and Induction Factor.**
Setting thrust equal to weight cancels density and area and relates the squared ratio of hover induced velocity to descent speed to the induction factor alone.

$$
\left( \frac{v_h}{V_d} \right)^{2} = a (1 - a)
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Momentum Theory Bound on the Descent Ratio.**
Because the induction factor term cannot exceed one quarter, momentum theory has a solution only when the descent speed is at least twice the hover induced velocity.

$$
\frac{V_d}{v_h} \geq 2
\tag{9}
$$

*Equation 10, Bespoke Autorotative Descent Rate of the X-25B.*
The measured autorotation ratio of 1.8 applied to the hover induced velocity at the assumed 350 pounds gives a descent of about 28 feet per second.

$$
V_d \approx 1.8 \, v_h = 1.8 (15.3) = 27.6 \, \text{ft/s} = 18.8 \, \text{mph}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Terminal Descent of a Drag Device.**
Balancing weight against the drag of a device with coefficient $C_D$ referred to swept area gives its terminal descent speed.

$$
W = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V_d^2 A \, C_D \quad \Longrightarrow \quad V_d = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{\rho A C_D}}
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Drag Coefficient Equivalent to a Descent Ratio.**
Substituting the definition of the hover induced velocity makes weight, density and area cancel, so a descent ratio fixes a drag coefficient on disc area.

$$
V_d = \frac{2 v_h}{\sqrt{C_D}} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad C_D = \frac{4}{(V_d / v_h)^2}
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Drag Coefficient of an Autorotating Rotor.**
The measured autorotation ratio of 1.8 corresponds to a drag coefficient of about 1.23 referred to disc area.

$$
C_D = \frac{4}{(1.8)^2} = 1.23
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Projected Area of an Inflated Canopy.**
The projected area of an inflated canopy is the nominal area scaled by the square of the ratio of projected to nominal diameter.
[Knacke's recovery systems design manual][book_knacke_1992]

$$
S_p = \left( \frac{D_p}{D_0} \right)^{2} S_0
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Canopy Drag Coefficient on Projected Area.**
A flat circular canopy coefficient of 0.75 on nominal area becomes about 1.67 on projected area when the inflated diameter is 0.67 of the nominal.
[Knacke's recovery systems design manual][book_knacke_1992]

$$
C_{D,\text{proj}} = \frac{0.75}{(0.67)^2} = 1.67
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Nominal Area of the Standard Personnel Canopy.**
The standard personnel canopy of 28 foot nominal diameter has a nominal area of about 616 square feet.
[Knacke's recovery systems design manual][book_knacke_1992]

$$
A_0 = \pi (14)^2 = 615.8 \, \text{ft}^2
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Disc or Canopy Loading.**
The loading of a swept-area drag device is its weight divided by its swept area.

$$
\frac{W}{A} = \text{disc loading, or canopy loading}
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Terminal Descent in Terms of Loading.**
The terminal descent speed of any swept-area drag device is a constant set by its drag coefficient times the square root of loading over density.

$$
V_d = k \sqrt{\frac{W / A}{\rho}}, \qquad k = \sqrt{\frac{2}{C_D}}
\tag{18}
$$

*Equation 19, Bespoke Equal-Weight Descent Ratio of Rotor to Canopy.*
At equal weight the rotor on the taken 20 foot disc descends about nine percent faster than the 28 foot canopy, a ratio from which the weight cancels.

$$
\frac{V_{\text{rotor}}}{V_{\text{canopy}}} = \sqrt{\frac{C_{D,c} A_c}{C_{D,r} A_r}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.75 \times 615.8}{1.23 \times 314.2}} = 1.091
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Glide Angle and Sink Rate.**
The glide angle has a tangent equal to the reciprocal of the lift-to-drag ratio and the sink rate is the airspeed times the sine of that angle.

$$
\tan\gamma = \frac{1}{L/D}, \qquad V_s = V \sin\gamma
\tag{20}
$$

*Equation 21, Bespoke Small-Angle Sink Rate in the Glide.*
Dividing a best-glide speed the article assumes as 45 miles an hour by an assumed lift-to-drag ratio of 4 gives a sink rate of 16.5 feet per second.

$$
V_s = \frac{V}{L/D} = \frac{66.0 \, \text{ft/s}}{4} = 16.5 \, \text{ft/s}
\tag{21}
$$

*Equation 22, Bespoke Exact Sink Rate in the Glide.*
The exact form at the same assumed speed and ratio gives 16.0 feet per second, so the simpler form reads three percent high.

$$
V_s = V \sin\gamma = 66.0 \sin(14.04^\circ) = 16.0 \, \text{ft/s}
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Still-Air Glide Range.**
In still air a glide at a fixed lift-to-drag ratio covers a horizontal range equal to the release height times that ratio.

$$
R = h \, (L/D)
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Descent Rate at Altitude in the Standard Atmosphere.**
The descent rate scales with the inverse square root of the density ratio, which the tropospheric standard atmosphere gives as a power law in height.

$$
V_d(h) = V_d(0) \sqrt{\frac{\rho_0}{\rho(h)}}, \qquad \frac{\rho(h)}{\rho_0} = \left( 1 - 6.875 \times 10^{-6} h \right)^{4.256}
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Time Aloft with Density Varying.**
Integrating the inverse sink rate over height, with the sink rate varying as the inverse square root of the density ratio, gives the time aloft.

$$
t = \int_{0}^{h} \frac{dz}{V_s(z)} = \frac{1}{V_s(0)} \int_{0}^{h} \sqrt{\frac{\rho(z)}{\rho_0}} \; dz
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Rotor Solidity.*
Two blades of an assumed 7 inch chord on the taken 10 foot radius give a solidity of about 0.037.

$$
\sigma = \frac{N c}{\pi R} = \frac{2 (0.583)}{\pi (10)} = 0.037
\tag{26}
$$

*Equation 27, Bespoke Canopy Area Matching the Rotor Drag Area.*
Matching the drag area of the taken rotor disc at the measured coefficient with fabric at 0.75 needs about 517 square feet of canopy.

$$
C_D A = 1.23 \times 314.2 = 388 \, \text{ft}^2, \qquad S_0 = \frac{388}{0.75} = 517 \, \text{ft}^2
\tag{27}
$$

*Equation 28, Bespoke Lock Number Definition and Blade Inertia.*
The Lock number compares aerodynamic forcing on a blade to its inertia, here with the inertia of a uniform blade of a mass the article assumes as 12 pounds.

$$
\gamma_L = \frac{\rho a c R^4}{I_b}, \qquad I_b = \tfrac{1}{3} m_b R^2 = 12.4 \, \text{slug ft}^2
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Lock Number of the X-25B Blade.*
At sea-level density with a lift-curve slope of 5.7, the assumed chord and the assumed blade inertia, the Lock number is about 6.4.

$$
\gamma_L = \frac{(0.002377)(5.7)(0.583)(10)^4}{12.4} = 6.4
\tag{29}
$$

*Equation 30, Bespoke Rotor Angular Speed.*
A tip speed the article assumes as 400 feet per second on a 10 foot radius gives 40 radians per second.

$$
\Omega = \frac{V_{tip}}{R} = \frac{400}{10} = 40 \, \text{rad/s} = 382 \, \text{rpm}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Thrust Coefficient.*
The assumed 350 pounds referred to the dynamic pressure at the assumed tip speed on the taken disc gives a thrust coefficient of about 0.0029.

$$
C_T = \frac{W}{\rho A (\Omega R)^2} = \frac{350}{(0.002377)(314.2)(400)^2} = 0.0029
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Blade Loading Coefficient.*
Dividing the thrust coefficient by the assumed solidity gives a blade loading coefficient of about 0.079, below the stall limit near 0.10.

$$
\frac{C_T}{\sigma} = \frac{0.0029}{0.037} = 0.079
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Tip Speed Ratio in Autorotation.*
The assumed tip speed over the modelled descent rate gives a tip speed ratio of about 14.5.

$$
\lambda = \frac{\Omega R}{V_d} = \frac{400}{27.6} = 14.5
\tag{33}
$$

*Equation 34, Bespoke Rotor Moment of Inertia.*
Treating each of the two blades as a uniform rod of the assumed mass about the hub gives about 25 slug square feet.

$$
I = N \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} m_b R^2 = 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} (0.373)(100) = 24.9 \, \text{slug ft}^2
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Stored Rotational Energy.*
The rotational kinetic energy of the assumed inertia at the assumed angular speed is about 19,900 foot-pounds.

$$
E = \tfrac{1}{2} I \Omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} (24.9)(40)^2 = 19{,}900 \, \text{ft lb}
\tag{35}
$$

*Equation 36, Bespoke Ideal Height Loss to Spin Up the Rotor.*
Dividing the stored energy by the assumed weight gives about 57 feet of height if every part of the potential energy went into the rotor.

$$
h = \frac{E}{W} = \frac{19{,}900}{350} = 57 \, \text{ft}
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Stored Energy Independent of Radius.*
For blades taken as uniform rods turning at a fixed tip speed, the stored energy reduces to the blade mass times the square of tip speed and the radius cancels.

$$
E = \tfrac{1}{2} I \Omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( N \tfrac{1}{3} m_b R^2 \right) \left( \frac{V_{tip}}{R} \right)^{2} = \frac{N}{6} m_b V_{tip}^2
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Descent Rate Scaling with Weight and Radius.**
Because the descent rate goes as the square root of disc loading, it scales as the square root of weight over the rotor radius.
[Kaman KSA-100 SAVER][ref_kaman_saver]

$$
V_d \propto \frac{\sqrt{W}}{R}
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Kinetic Energy of the Descent.**
The energy a flare must absorb is the kinetic energy of the vehicle at its descent rate.

$$
E_{req} = \tfrac{1}{2} \frac{W}{g} V_d^2
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Flare Energy Required in Terms of Weight and Radius.**
Substituting the measured descent ratio of 1.8 and the actuator-disc induced velocity makes the required energy go as the square of weight over the square of radius.

$$
E_{req} = \frac{(1.8)^2}{2 g \rho \pi} \cdot \frac{W^2}{R^2}
\tag{40}
$$

*Equation 41, Bespoke Flare Energy Margin.*
The article defines the margin as the stored energy of uniform-rod blades over the energy the flare requires.

$$
\frac{E_{avail}}{E_{req}} = \frac{N m_b V_{tip}^2 \, g \rho \pi R^2}{3 (1.8)^2 W^2}
\tag{41}
$$

*Equation 42, Bespoke Blade Mass for a Unit Energy Margin.*
Inverting the margin at unity gives the blade mass a rotor would need, 2.5 pounds a blade for the X-25B and 21 for the Stowable Aircrew Vehicle Escape Rotorseat, or SAVER, against the assumed 12.

$$
m_b = \frac{3 (1.8)^2 W^2}{N V_{tip}^2 g \rho \pi R^2}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Thrust-to-Weight Ratio of the SAVER.**
The documented 430 pound turbofan thrust over the 710 pound SAVER weight is a thrust-to-weight ratio of 0.61.
[Kaman KSA-100 SAVER][ref_kaman_saver]

$$
\frac{T}{W} = \frac{430}{710} = 0.61
\tag{43}
$$

*Equation 44, Bespoke Stored Energy of a Small Lift Rotor.*
The uniform-rod stored energy in terms of blade count, blade mass and tip speed shows that a small light blade at modest tip speed stores little energy.

$$
E = \frac{N}{6} m_b V_{tip}^2
\tag{44}
$$

### Notation

- $\phi$, the inflow angle at a blade element
- $C_d$, the section drag coefficient, with $C_l$ the section lift coefficient
- $R$, the rotor radius, and in Equation 23 the glide range
- $A$, the rotor disc area, or the swept area of a drag device
- $v_h$, the hover induced velocity
- $W$, the weight
- $\rho$, the air density, with $\rho_0$ its sea-level value
- $V_d$, the descent rate
- $a$, the induction factor, and in Equations 28 and 29 the lift-curve slope
- $C_D$, the drag coefficient referred to swept area
- $D_p$, the projected diameter of an inflated canopy, with $D_0$ the nominal diameter
- $S_0$, the nominal area of a canopy, with $S_p$ the projected area
- $k$, the descent constant of a swept-area drag device
- $\gamma$, the glide angle
- $V_s$, the sink rate in the glide
- $\sigma$, the rotor solidity
- $N$, the number of blades
- $c$, the blade chord
- $\gamma_L$, the Lock number
- $I_b$, the moment of inertia of one blade about the hub, with $I$ that of the rotor
- $m_b$, the mass of one blade
- $\Omega$, the rotor angular speed
- $V_{tip}$, the blade tip speed
- $C_T$, the thrust coefficient
- $\lambda$, the tip speed ratio
- $E_{req}$, the energy a flare must absorb, with $E_{avail}$ the stored rotor energy
